content:
We have carbon NMR data: chemical shifts: 168.60, 143.85, 130.30, 22.80, 21.35, 19.20. Aromatic carbons typically appear around 110-160 ppm. Here we have three peaks in that region: 168.60 (maybe carbonyl), 143.85, 130.30. 168.60 could be carbonyl (C=O) of aromatic acid or amide. Aromatic carbons are usually 110-150. So 143.85 and 130.30 are aromatic. Possibly also 168.60 if it's aromatic carbon attached to electron-withdrawing group (e.g., carbonyl carbon of aromatic acid). But typical carbonyl carbon appears ~170-200. So likely not aromatic. So number of aromatic carbons = 2.

But we need to be sure. Could there be more aromatic carbons not observed? The sample may have more carbons but only 6 signals observed, maybe symmetry reduces number. The low-field peaks 22.80,21.35,19.20 are aliphatic methyls. So total carbons = 6 distinct signals. If aromatic ring has 6 carbons, symmetry could reduce to 2 signals (e.g., para-disubstituted benzene gives 4 signals? Actually para-disubstituted gives 4 distinct aromatic carbons). But we only have 2 aromatic signals. Could be 1,4-disubstituted with symmetry giving 2 sets of equivalent carbons (two pairs). That would be 4 aromatic carbons but only 2 signals. However the question asks number of aromatic carbons in the molecule, not number of distinct aromatic carbon signals. So we need to infer the actual count.

We need more info: maybe we can get HSQC to see which protons attached. Let's get HSQC.
